passages.title: Harbor Morning
passages.text: The ship and the sheep share the same shore this morning

passages.title: Harbor Morning
passages.text: This morning the ship sits quiet in the harbor while sheep graze on the green hill above the shore. A child points at the sheep then at the ship and laughs because the two words sound almost the same in her mind. The guide asks her to say ship when she means the boat and sheep when she means the animals. Clear speech matters here because a wrong vowel can send a listener looking at the wrong thing. Practice the short vowel in ship and the longer vowel in sheep until both feel easy.

passages.title: River Light
passages.text: A light rain ran along the long river road

passages.title: River Light
passages.text: A light rain ran along the long river road while riders raced toward the old bridge. On the left a large red lantern glowed. On the right a row of low houses reflected in the water. Really clear speech helps a stranger tell left from right and long from wrong without guessing. Read slowly through the liquid sounds and keep the tongue tip light for l and more curled for r. When you finish, compare how river and liver would change the whole scene if one letter slipped.

passages.title: Think Thanks
passages.text: They think the thick thread is thinner than that

passages.title: Think Thanks
passages.text: They think the thick thread is thinner than that cloth their mother chose for the theater curtain. Throughout the afternoon those three friends thank each other with thoughtful words rather than gifts. The difference between think and this or between breath and breathe can hide in a soft tongue between the teeth. Practice both the quiet th and the voiced th until neither collapses into a simple t or d. Then read the whole paragraph again without rushing the endings.

passages.title: Vivid Waves
passages.text: We view the vivid waves with very wide eyes

passages.title: Vivid Waves
passages.text: We view the vivid waves with very wide eyes while a west wind moves over the water. Every visitor wants a photograph of the velvet evening light on the harbor. Keep v and w distinct so vine and wine do not collapse into one word. Walk the wet stones and watch the water veer around the rocks. When you finish, say very and weary once more so the lip shape feels different each time.

passages.title: Park Bench
passages.text: Please put the big bag by the park bench

passages.title: Park Bench
passages.text: Please put the big bag by the park bench before people begin to pack the bus. A pale blue balloon pops beside a pile of brown paper cups. Pair and bear can confuse listeners if the first sound is not clear. Pick up the bread, pack the berries, and bring both back before the picnic begins. Read the whole scene once without stopping to fix every pop or bang.

passages.title: Record Progress
passages.text: Please record the record and present the present

passages.title: Record Progress
passages.text: Please record the record and present the present before you protest the protest. Object to the object if the stress lands on the wrong syllable. English often moves stress when a word changes from verb to noun, so a listener waits for that shift. Permit the permit to sit on the desk while you content yourself with the content of the letter. Read it through as one thought, then say each pair again with the beat in the right place.

passages.title: Make a Decision
passages.text: They make a decision and take a break before they do the work

passages.title: Make a Decision
passages.text: They make a decision and take a break before they do the work that really needs attention. Later they pay attention to the feedback and make an effort to improve without making excuses. Formulaic chunks like take a break and pay attention help speech move forward when searching for single words feels slow. Read the whole passage as connected speech rather than stopping after every phrase. When you finish, notice which chunks felt automatic and which still needed planning time.

passages.title: Busy Cities
passages.text: Busy cities buzz as buses zip past the shops

passages.title: Busy Cities
passages.text: Busy cities buzz as buses zip past the shops and offices close for the evening. Voices rise and fall while musicians play jazz beside the plaza. Listen for the soft s and the buzzing z in places like buses and buzz, or sip and zip. Some days the streets seem noisier because so many sounds sit close together. Read the scene once more and let the endings stay clear without turning every z into an s.

passages.title: Bad Bed
passages.text: The bad bed had a red blanket and a black bag

passages.title: Bad Bed
passages.text: The bad bed had a red blanket and a black bag beside a metal pan. He said he slept better after he left that flat and found a better bed. Keep bad and bed apart so a listener does not hear the wrong story. A man sat on the edge, then set his hat on the desk and checked the map again. Read it through without letting every open vowel collapse into the same sound.

passages.title: Singing Rain
passages.text: The singing rain ran down the green hanging vines

passages.title: Singing Rain
passages.text: The singing rain ran down the green hanging vines while children were singing along. Something in the evening air made the song feel longer than the night. Notice the ending of sing versus sin and of hanging versus handing. A thin ring of light hung over the lawn as the rain kept coming. Read the whole paragraph and let the ng land in the back of the mouth instead of turning into a plain n.

passages.title: Evening Walk
passages.text: On an evening walk by the river we view vivid lights while a light rain runs along the long road. A ship sits near the shore and sheep rest on the hill. They think the thick fog is thinner than it was this morning. Please put the big bag by the park bench before we make a decision and take a break. Busy voices buzz as buses pass and someone records a short record of the scene. Read this mixed passage at a calm pace and keep going forward even if one word feels hard.

passages.title: Office Morning
passages.text: Before the meeting they present the present and then record the record of who will speak first. People put paper by the bench and bring a black bag with a bad habit of spilling pens. She wants very wide windows so the west light can fill the room. Whether they thank each other or think aloud, the conversation still needs clear sounds. This office scene lets you practice several contrasts in one continuous read without stopping to fix every word.

passages.title: Free Three
passages.text: Three friends thought they were free to walk through the thick fog before the first ferry left. Fred thanked them for the thoughtful gift of fresh bread and three thin fish. Free and three can fall together if the tongue never finds the teeth. Follow the path, feel the frost, and think of the difference between first and thirst. Read it once more without turning every th into an f.

passages.title: Shore Choice
passages.text: She chose the ship by the shore, then watched children chase shells across the wet sand. A cheap chip of china sat in a dish beside the chair. Share and chair, ship and chip, wash and watch all ask for a small change in how the air leaves. Choose each word on purpose as you pass the shops and the church. Keep going until the hush of sh and the catch of ch feel like two different doors.

passages.title: Time and Dime
passages.text: It is time to drop a dime in the tin and take the ticket down to the dock. Two tired drivers tried to tie the door while the tide pulled at the boat. Time and dime, two and do, try and dry can blur if the first sound is too soft. Tell the tale, then do it again with a clearer tap at the start of each word. Do not stop to grade yourself. Just keep the story moving to the end.

passages.title: Quiet Kitchen
passages.text: In the quiet kitchen she heats the kettle, then cuts thick bread and sets three plates by the window. The recipe asks for fresh fish, a pinch of salt, and a little butter in the pan. Keep the rhythm easy as you read the steps, even when a word feels crowded. Stir, taste, and then wait while the steam rises from the pot. This is a simple morning scene. Let the sentences land without rushing the last sound of each one.

passages.title: Saturday Market
passages.text: Saturday morning the market fills with baskets of berries, bunches of basil, and bright paper bags. Buyers bargain a little, then pay and pack their things before the rain returns. A vendor calls out the price of bread while a boy balances a box of beans. Walk the lane once in your mind and name what you see without skipping the small words. When the crowd gets loud, keep your own pace. Finish the last stall before you look up.

passages.title: Quiet Library
passages.text: The library is quiet except for the soft slide of books back onto the long low shelves. A reader lifts a light volume, then writes a little note about the last chapter. Please leave the place as you found it. Put the paper by the desk and bring the borrowed book to the front before you leave. Listen for l and r in library, reader, and really as you move through the room. Then sit, breathe, and finish the page you started.

passages.title: Late Train
passages.text: The late train sits still at the station while people check the time and shift their bags. A ticket taker tells them the next departure will take ten minutes more. Stay, wait, then take a seat when the doors open. Some travelers talk too fast. Some stay silent and watch the rain on the glass. Read this as one continuous wait, not a list of delays, and keep the t sounds from turning into d.

passages.title: Green Garden
passages.text: Green beans grow along the garden wall while a girl gathers grapes in a gray basket. The ground is still wet from last night, so she goes slowly between the rows. Grow, go, girl, and grapes all start with a sound that needs a little voice. Keep that voice on and let the words feel full. When you reach the gate, go back to the first line and read the whole garden again without stopping to name every plant.

passages.title: Winter Window
passages.text: Winter light sits on the wide window while wind moves the white curtains. We wait with wool sweaters and watch the weather turn. Wide, wait, wind, and weather ask for a round lip without biting the sound. Very little happens in this room, which is the point. Stay with the quiet picture until the last word, then look out the window once more and say the first sentence as if you were still seeing it.
